a: I gained a holding
p: Vaticanus says Wisdom "acquired" a share in every nation; a corrector of Sinaiticus says she "led".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete

readings.plain: I gained a holding

readings.w: a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc.a), in Swete's notes
readings.en: I led, I ruled
readings.plain: I took the lead

why: The Plain follows Swete's text; the corrector's reading is a single later change, and "gained a holding" prepares for 24:7–8, where Wisdom looks for an inheritance and receives Israel.

a: on the seashore
t: On the seashore, or at En-gedi?
p: Vaticanus has "on the beaches". A corrector of Sinaiticus has "in En-gedi", the oasis by the Dead Sea, which the KJV follows.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: on the beaches
readings.plain: on the seashore

readings.w: a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc.a), in Swete's notes; codex 248 has ἐν Γαδδί, as Hart (1909) prints it; the KJV ("in En-gaddi")
readings.en: in En-gedi
readings.plain: at En-gedi

why: The Plain keeps Swete's text. The other reading is attractive, since the list names places in the land (Lebanon, Hermon, Jericho) and En-gedi's vineyards are praised in the Song of Songs (Song of Songs 1:14), and the two Greek words look alike; but in the great codices it is found only in a correction.

a: [I am the mother of beautiful love, / of fear, of knowledge and of holy hope. / And with all my children I give what lasts forever / to those he has named.]
p: Not in Vaticanus. Codex 248 has the whole verse; the Latin has its first half (Vulgate 24:24).

readings.w: Codex 248 (a minuscule manuscript), as Hart (1909) prints it (page 33); Hart's apparatus reports both halves in minuscule 70 too
readings.orig: ἐγὼ μήτηρ τῆς ἀγαπήσεως τῆς καλῆς καὶ φόβου καὶ γνώσεως καὶ τῆς ὁσίας ἐλπίδος, δίδωμι δὲ σὺν πᾶσι τοῖς τέκνοις μου ἀειγενεῖς τοῖς λεγομένοις ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ.
readings.en: I am the mother of beautiful love and of fear and knowledge and holy hope; and I give, with all my children, ever-living (things?), to those spoken of by him
readings.plain: [I am the mother of beautiful love, / of fear, of knowledge and of holy hope. / And with all my children I give what lasts forever / to those he has named.]

readings.orig: δίδομαι οὖν πᾶσι τοῖς τέκνοις μου ἀειγενεῖς τοῖς λεγομένοις ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ (second half)
readings.en: so I am given to all my children, the ever-living ones, to those spoken of by him
readings.plain: [I am the mother of beautiful love, / of fear, of knowledge and of holy hope. / So I am given to all my children, / ever-living, to those he has named.]

readings.w: Latin, Clementine Vulgate 24:24 (first half only); the Douay-Rheims ("I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope")

readings.en: I am the mother of beautiful love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope.
readings.plain: [I am the mother of beautiful love, / of fear, of knowledge and of holy hope.]

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, as Swete prints them, lack it too
readings.en: (no verse)

why: Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have no verse 18, but the KJV and most English Bibles use the number, so the Plain gives the line in brackets, translated from codex 248 as Hart prints it. The first half also stands in the Latin; the second half has no Latin.
b: The second half is hard Greek. In 248 the verb is active, "I give", and sun, "with", stands before "all my children"; aeigeneis, "ever-living", has no noun with it, so the Plain supplies "what". Hart suggests the line was translated from a Hebrew source in which the word read as "with" was the Hebrew object marker (et), giving "I give all my eternal fruits to God's elect". Minuscule 70, as Hart reports it, has the passive "So I am given to all my children", the form behind the KJV. The note on "the mother of beautiful love" tells how the Latin line became a title of Mary.

a: the law Moses commanded
p: Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus add "us": "the law Moses commanded us".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete

readings.plain: the law Moses commanded

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (ℵ, A), in Swete's notes; Hart's apparatus (1909) adds minuscules 55, 70, 155, 248, 253 and 254

readings.plain: the law Moses commanded us

readings.w: Codex 248 (a minuscule manuscript), as Hart (1909) prints it (page 33)

readings.plain: the law Moses commanded us

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. The meaning is the same; "us" brings the line closer to Deuteronomy 33:4, which it quotes: "Moses commanded us a law, the heritage of the assembly of Jacob" (Deuteronomy 33:4). The KJV, like Vaticanus, has no "us".
b: Codex 248 has the heading "From Deuteronomy" (Ἐκ τοῦ δευτερονομίου) just before this line; Hart's commentary says that 248 "supplies the reference" to the verse quoted. It also has "law" in the nominative and "in the assemblies".

a: [Do not give up being strong in the Lord, / so that he himself will make you strong; cling to him. / The Lord Almighty alone is God, / and besides him there is no other savior.]
p: Not in Vaticanus or the Latin. Codex 248 and minuscule 70 have it; the KJV follows it.

readings.w: Codex 248 (a minuscule manuscript), as Hart (1909) prints it (page 33)

readings.en: Do not give up being strong in the Lord, so that he himself may strengthen you; cling to him. The Lord Almighty alone is God, and there is no other savior besides him.
readings.plain: [Do not give up being strong in the Lord, / so that he himself will make you strong; cling to him. / The Lord Almighty alone is God, / and besides him there is no other savior.]

readings.w: Minuscule 70, as Hart's apparatus (1909) reports it: ἰσχύν, "strength", for ἰσχύειν, and "but cling to him" (κολλᾶσθε δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν) placed before "so that he will make you strong"
readings.orig: μὴ ἐκλύεσθε ἰσχὺν ἐν Κυρίῳ, κολλᾶσθε δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν, ἵνα κραταιώσῃ ὑμᾶς αὐτός
readings.en: Do not let your strength give way in the Lord, but cling to him, so that he himself may strengthen you
readings.plain: [Do not let your strength give way in the Lord, / but cling to him, so that he will make you strong. / The Lord Almighty alone is God, / and besides him there is no other savior.]

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, as Swete prints them, lack it too
readings.en: (no verse)

why: The great codices lack the verse, and the Latin has nothing like it here; the KJV numbers it 24:24. The Plain gives it in brackets, translated from codex 248 as Hart prints it.
b: Hart reports the verse only in the minuscules 70 and 248 and calls it an exhortation based on Deuteronomy 33. A Greek anthology he cites has its first line in 248's form. It is the only line in this chapter addressed to "you" (plural).

a: a man who has joy in his children
t: Joy in his children, or in his end?
p: The Greek says the happy man has joy in his children. The Hebrew of Manuscript C says he rejoices "in his end".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: a person rejoicing in children
readings.plain: a man who has joy in his children

readings.w: Hebrew, Cairo Genizah Manuscript C, folio VI verso, lines 11–12 (Elizur's transcription)
readings.orig: אשרי איש שמח באחריתו חי וראה בשבר צריו
readings.en: happy is the man who rejoices in his end (his last days, or what comes after him), who lives and sees the fall of his foes
readings.plain: a man who has joy in how his life ends

why: The Plain translates the Greek. The Hebrew word acharit means the end or the last part, which can be a man's old age or the children who come after him; the Greek has "children", which may be how its translator understood the word, or may rest on a different Hebrew copy.

a: who shares his home with a wife of understanding
t: The Hebrew adds the ox and the donkey
p: Manuscript C adds, "and he who does not plow with an ox and a donkey together", and puts the lines in another order.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: happy the one living with a wife of understanding
readings.plain: who shares his home with a wife of understanding

readings.w: Hebrew, Cairo Genizah Manuscript C, folio VII recto, lines 2–4 (Abegg's transcription; the last letters of the last word are marked as uncertain)
readings.orig: אשרי בעל אשה משכלת ולא חורש כשור עם חמוׄר
readings.en: happy is the husband of a sensible wife, and he who does not plow with an ox and a donkey together
readings.plain: who is the husband of a wife of understanding, and who does not plow with an ox and a donkey together

why: The Plain translates the Greek. The Hebrew line is old and vivid: it borrows the law against yoking an ox with a donkey (Deuteronomy 22:10) as a picture of a mismatched marriage. The Greek either did not have it or left it out.

a: The fear of the Lord goes beyond everything.
t: The fear, or the love, of the Lord?

why: The Plain follows the Greek of the great codices. The KJV's form is that of codex 248; it fits 25:12, which in 248 speaks of loving him.

a: an enemy's anger
t: An enemy's anger, or a woman's?
p: The Greek says no anger is worse than an enemy's. The Latin has "a woman's".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree, as Swete prints them
readings.en: the anger of an enemy
readings.plain: an enemy's anger

readings.w: Latin, Clementine Vulgate 25:23
readings.en: the anger of a woman
readings.plain: a woman's anger

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Latin's "woman" ties the line to the poem on the evil wife that follows; but the Greek pair "snake" and "enemy" makes sense as it stands, and no Hebrew of this verse has been found.

a: it makes her face as dark as sackcloth
p: Vaticanus has "like sackcloth". Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have "like a bear", and so does the Hebrew.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: σκοτοῖ τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτῆς ὡς σάκκον
readings.en: darkens her face like sackcloth
readings.plain: it makes her face as dark as sackcloth

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (ℵ, A), in Swete's notes; codex 248, as Hart (1909) prints it
readings.en: like a bear
readings.plain: it makes her face as dark as a bear's

readings.w: Hebrew, Cairo Genizah Manuscript C, folio VII recto, lines 7–9 (Abegg's transcription: a gap in the leaf after the first line; the yod of "his face" is restored by Abegg)
readings.orig: רע אשה ישחיר [ -- ] מראה איש ויקדיר פנ[י]וׄ לדוב
readings.en: a woman's evil blackens [gap] a man's looks and darkens his face like a bear
readings.plain: it blackens a man's looks and makes his face as dark as a bear's

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. "Bear" is very likely the older reading, since the Hebrew has it; sackcloth, dark goat-hair cloth worn in mourning, may be a copyist's change to an easier picture. The Hebrew also makes the husband's face, not the wife's, go dark, which fits 25:18.

a: and hearing it, he groans bitterly
t: Hearing it, or without meaning to?
p: The Greek says he groans "when he hears". The Hebrew says he sighs "without his will", before he can stop himself.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and having heard, he groaned bitterly
readings.plain: and hearing it, he groans bitterly

readings.w: Hebrew, Cairo Genizah Manuscript C, folio VII recto, line 10 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.en: and without his intending it, he sighs
readings.plain: and without meaning to, he sighs

why: The Plain translates the Greek. The Hebrew uvlo' ta'mo means "without his sense, his choosing": the husband cannot help sighing. The grandson may have read a different word or guessed.

a: and do not set your longing on a woman
t: Longing for her, or for her money?
p: The Greek warns against longing for a woman. The Hebrew warns against hurrying to her because of what she owns.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and do not long for a woman
readings.plain: and do not set your longing on a woman

readings.w: Hebrew, Cairo Genizah Manuscript C, folio VII verso, lines 3–4 (Abegg's transcription; the first letter of "do not" is restored by Abegg)
readings.en: and for what she has, do not hurry
readings.plain: and do not rush after her for what she owns

why: The Plain translates the Greek. The Hebrew line goes with 25:22, where a rich wife who keeps her husband brings him shame: do not marry for beauty or for money.

a: power to do as she likes
p: Vaticanus has "authority". Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have "freedom of speech".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: nor authority to an evil woman
readings.plain: power to do as she likes

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (ℵ, A), in Swete's notes

readings.plain: freedom to go out as she likes

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. "Freedom of speech" fits the busy tongue of 25:20 and the leak of water in the first line; "authority" fits the next verse, where she will not "walk as your hand guides her". Codex 248's "freedom to go out" is the source of the KJV's "gad abroad".

p: The KJV adds "and give her a bill of divorce, and let her go".

readings.plain: cut her away from your flesh, so that she does not keep abusing you.

why: The Plain follows the Greek of the great codices. Codex 248 adds "give and send away", which the KJV expands to "give her a bill of divorce"; the extra words spell out what "cut her away from your flesh" already means, using the language of Deuteronomy 24:1.

a: in front of a fourth I plead for help
p: Vaticanus says "I pleaded" at the fourth thing. A corrector of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus say "I was afraid".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete

readings.plain: in front of a fourth I plead for help

readings.w: A corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc.a) and Codex Alexandrinus (A), in Swete's notes (the first hand of Sinaiticus has ἐδόθην, "I was given"); codex 248 (Hart 1909)

readings.plain: before a fourth I am afraid

why: The Plain follows Swete's text, though "I was afraid" matches the first line ("my heart shrinks back") and the Latin (facies mea metuit, "my face feared"); the three Greek verbs look alike, and Vaticanus may have a copyist's slip.

a: Keep an unbending watch over a daughter
t: An unbending watch, or a headstrong daughter?
p: In Vaticanus the word is an adverb, "unbendingly". In Alexandrinus it describes the daughter: "headstrong".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: over a daughter firmly set a guard
readings.plain: Keep an unbending watch over a daughter

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and others, in Swete's notes and Hart's apparatus (1909); codex 248, as Hart prints it

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), in Hart's apparatus (1909)

readings.plain: Keep a firm watch over a headstrong daughter

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. In Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus the word ends in -ō and describes the daughter, not the watch; Sinaiticus spells it with one more letter. That form fits 26:11's "shameless eye" and the Latin in filia non avertente se, "a daughter who does not turn herself away"; Vaticanus makes the line a general rule for any daughter.

a: in the order of his house

p: Goes with 26:19–27: in codex 248 (and, as Hart reports, minuscule 70 and the Syriac), not in the great codices or the Latin. It ends with the saying of 26:1.

a: [A loud woman with a busy tongue / will be looked on as fit to put enemies to flight. / The soul of every person who is like these / will live out life in the turmoil of war.]
p: Goes with 26:19–27. Codex 248 and minuscule 70 differ in the first line: 70 adds "like a trumpet".

readings.en: A loud-voiced and talkative woman will be regarded for the rout of enemies. The soul of every person of like ways to these will spend life in the disorders of war.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, as Swete prints them, lack it too
readings.en: (no verse)

why: Part of the passage 26:19–27 (see 26:19). The Plain follows codex 248 as Hart prints it. Its first line is terse: "will be looked on for the rout of enemies", that is, her voice would scare off an army. The KJV takes it the same way: "shall be sought out to drive away the enemies". Minuscule 70's "like a trumpet" makes the noise itself the picture. The KJV has only the first line.

a: for something of no real value
p: Vaticanus says many sinned over "something indifferent", a trifle. Sinaiticus' first hand says "for profit"; the Latin, "because of poverty".

readings.en: for the sake of something indifferent
readings.plain: for something of no real value

why: The Plain follows Swete's text, which the KJV also took this way ("for a small matter"). Sinaiticus' first hand, a corrector of which restored Vaticanus' word, fits the second line about getting rich; the two words differ by one letter.

a: at his own expense
t: At a cost, or for nothing?
p: Vaticanus says the lender gained an enemy "not for free": it cost him his money. Other copies drop "not": an enemy "for no reason".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: he gained him as an enemy, not for nothing
readings.plain: at his own expense

readings.w: A corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc.a) and Codex Alexandrinus (A), in Swete's notes and Hart's apparatus (1909); codex 248, as Hart prints it (δωρεὰν ἐχθρόν); the Latin (Vulgate 29:8, gratis)
readings.en: he gained him as an enemy for nothing
readings.plain: for no reason

why: The Plain follows Swete's text: the lender has lost his money and made an enemy, so the enemy came at a price. Without "not", the line says the lender did nothing to deserve the hatred. Both make sense.

a: Many have refused to lend because of such wickedness
p: The Greek says many refuse to lend because of borrowers' wickedness. The Latin says they refuse "not out of wickedness" but from fear.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: many, on account of wickedness, have turned away
readings.plain: Many have refused to lend because of such wickedness

readings.w: Latin, Clementine Vulgate 29:10; the Douay-Rheims ("Many have refused to lend, not out of wickedness, but they were afraid to be defrauded without cause")
readings.orig: Multi non causa nequitiae non foenerati sunt
readings.en: many have not lent, not out of wickedness
readings.plain: Many have refused to lend, not out of wickedness

why: The Plain follows the Greek: the borrowers' bad faith (29:4–6) makes people stop lending. The Latin defends the lenders: they are not mean, only afraid.

a: and do not keep him waiting for alms
p: Swete's Vaticanus lacks "not", which makes the line say the opposite. The Plain follows the copies that have it.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (ℵ, A) and others, as Hart's apparatus (1909) reports them; codex 248, as Hart prints it (καὶ ἐπὶ ἐλεημοσύνῃ μὴ παρελκύσῃς αὐτόν); the Latin (Vulgate 29:11, non trahas illum)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἐλεημοσύνην μὴ παρελκύσῃς αὐτόν
readings.en: and do not put him off for alms
readings.plain: and do not keep him waiting for alms

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and for alms you will put him off
readings.plain: and you will keep him waiting for alms

why: Here the Plain departs from Swete's base text. Without "not" the line contradicts its own first half ("be patient with a person in a low position") and the verses that follow (29:9–13). The negative is in Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, codex 248 and the Latin, so its loss in Vaticanus is best explained as a copyist's slip.
b: The first reading's Greek is Vaticanus' wording with the negative; Swete's notes add that Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have the dative ἐλεημοσύνῃ and Alexandrinus ἐπί, which do not change the sense.

a: Be satisfied with a little or a lot.
p: Vaticanus has one line. Codex 248, a corrector of Sinaiticus and the Latin add a second.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐπὶ μικρῷ καὶ μεγάλῳ εὐδοκίαν ἔχε.
readings.en: with little and much have contentment
readings.plain: Be satisfied with a little or a lot.

readings.w: Codex 248 (a minuscule manuscript), as Hart (1909) prints it (page 40); a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc.a), in Hart's apparatus; the KJV ("Be it little or much, hold thee contented, that thou hear not the reproach of thy house")
readings.orig: ἐπὶ μικρὰ καὶ μεγάλα εὐδοκίαν ἔχε, καὶ ὀνειδισμὸν οἰκίας σου μὴ ἀκούσῃς.
readings.en: with little and much have contentment, and do not hear the reproach of your house
readings.plain: Be satisfied with a little or a lot, so that you do not hear your household insulted.

readings.w: Latin, Clementine Vulgate 29:30
readings.orig: Minimum pro magno placeat tibi, et improperium peregrinationis non audies.
readings.en: Let the least please you as much as the great, and you will not hear the reproach of being a stranger.
readings.plain: Be satisfied with a little or a lot, and you will not hear yourself insulted as a lodger.

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. The second line leads well into 29:24–28, about the insults a lodger must hear; it may have been added to round off the couplet, or lost from Vaticanus. Where 248 has "your house", the Latin has "your being a stranger".
